title: Beyond Zero: Google Publishes Successor to BeyondCorp
gist: Google published a research paper on 'Beyond Zero,' a successor to its 2014 BeyondCorp zero-trust model that extends continuous, resource-level authorization to autonomous AI agents acting at machine speed, but critics call it aspirational and warn that non-deterministic AI decisions are a poor fit for hard security boundaries.

insights.claim: Beyond Zero moves access-control decisions from the application level down to individual resources and actions, combining static authorization policies with dynamic AI-driven decisions to enable machine-speed enforcement for both humans and AI agents.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Signals a structural shift in enterprise security architecture toward per-action authorization, which vendors and security-tooling companies will need to build products around.

insights.claim: Beyond Zero is built on five principles: authorization at the level of individual actions and resources across interfaces and APIs; a mix of static policies and dynamic controls for higher-risk scenarios; automatically enriched context about users, actions, data, and risk; automated investigation triggered by risk signals; and challenges or containment measures requiring extra verification or telemetry from humans and AI agents.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete checklist investors and security architects can use to evaluate whether a vendor's product actually implements action-level, risk-based authorization versus legacy app-level access control.
insights.locator: Beyond Zero uses contextual and risk-based, resource-level controls

insights.claim: Google's paper authors argue that BeyondCorp's founding assumptions—that accessors are human, actions occur at human speed, and applications are the right trust boundary—no longer hold in an era of autonomous AI agents.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Frames AI agents as an architectural discontinuity for enterprise security, not an incremental feature, which justifies fresh spend on identity/access infrastructure built for machine-speed actors.
insights.quote: The assumptions underpinning BeyondCorp — that accessors are human, that actions occur at human speed, and that applications are the correct boundary for trust—are no longer sufficient.
insights.locator: Joseph Valente, formerly director of product management at Google, and Michal Zalewski

insights.claim: Google published the original BeyondCorp whitepaper in 2014, establishing zero-trust access as a replacement for network-perimeter security in the enterprise.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Google has a 12-year track record of publishing security models that later became industry standards, giving Beyond Zero more credibility as a future benchmark than a typical vendor whitepaper.
insights.locator: In 2014, Google published the BeyondCorp whitepaper

insights.claim: Joseph Valente says Google built continuous per-action authorization internally well before the rest of the industry, and it only became necessary at scale once hundreds of thousands of human workers were joined by millions of AI agents.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Suggests the agent-population growth curve inside large tech companies is already forcing security re-architecture, a leading indicator for what mid-size enterprises will need to handle next.
insights.quote: Beyond Zero is one of those areas where Google had built something internally that was well ahead of anyone else for a long time. Doing continuous authorization of every action at scale seemed like overkill at first. But then thousands of workers became hundreds of thousands of workers. Hundreds of thousands of workers were joined by millions of agents. And so on...

insights.claim: Google security leaders Heather Adkins and Archana Ramamoorthy frame the shift as a new era in which AI agents are being deployed globally to increase operational velocity and boost productivity, changing the assumptions underlying enterprise security.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Positions AI-agent deployment as an operational-velocity driver, which is the business case enterprises will cite when justifying investment in new access-control infrastructure.
insights.quote: The enterprise landscape is now entering a new era shaped by artificial intelligence, where AI is changing the assumptions around how enterprise security works. AI agents are being deployed globally to increase operational velocity and boost productivity.
insights.locator: Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, and Archana Ramamoorthy, senior director at Google, explain

themes.theme: Adoption barriers for the rest of the industry

insights.claim: For enterprises to adopt Beyond Zero, SaaS vendors will need to expose action-level authorization interfaces and industry standards will need to mature, which are not yet in place.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete gap—lack of SaaS-side action-level authorization APIs—that could become a product opportunity for identity and security vendors.
insights.locator: To adopt the latest model, SaaS vendors will need to expose action-level authorization

insights.claim: Smaller security teams face difficult practical issues in adopting Beyond Zero-style controls, including false positives, determining intent, auditing, and cost.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Suggests the model will likely be adopted first by large, well-resourced organizations, delaying broad market impact and creating a multi-year rollout curve for vendors targeting SMBs.
insights.locator: smaller security teams face difficult issues around false positives, intent, auditing, and cost

insights.claim: Kane Narraway, security manager at Canva, is supportive of Beyond Zero's goals but skeptical that ordinary enterprises can implement the model as quickly as Google suggests, since Google's own deployments remain internal-only and not all components are built.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A practitioner at a real enterprise (not Google) publicly cautions that the paper is a roadmap, not a deployable product, tempering near-term investment and vendor hype cycles.
insights.quote: It’s worth being clear about what this paper is and isn’t though. It’s aspirational. Google says deployments are internal-only, the components aren’t all built, and more papers are coming. This is the same playbook as 2014: publish the vision, describe the architecture at a high level, and encourage the industry to build towards it collaboratively (...) You aren’t Google and don’t try to be.
insights.locator: In the article "Beyond Zero: For The Rest Of Us," Kane Narraway

insights.claim: Community reaction on Hacker News to Beyond Zero has been largely skeptical, with commenters questioning the reliability and complexity of AI-driven authorization decisions.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Public developer sentiment is an early signal of adoption resistance that could slow enterprise buy-in even if the technical model is sound.
insights.locator: The community reaction on Hacker News has been so far largely skeptical

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter using the handle stogot argues that zero trust is inherently deterministic while AI is non-deterministic, making non-deterministic access controls a fundamentally bad security design.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Captures the core technical objection to AI-driven security models: probabilistic decision-making conflicts with the hard-boundary guarantees security teams expect from access control.
insights.quote: Zero trust is deterministic. AI is non-deterministic. Non-deterministic access controls are a terrible idea.

insights.claim: Commentator Firas Durri argues that preparing for AI agents in enterprise systems means expanding auditability and reversibility in software, not just adding new authorization layers.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Offers an alternative design principle—auditability and reversibility—that could be a differentiator for security tooling vendors competing against pure authorization-layer approaches.
insights.quote: Preparing for AI agents means expanding auditability and reversibility in software.

insights.claim: Google describes Beyond Zero as an ongoing effort and plans to publish further details on implementation and operational considerations, but has not given any specific deadlines.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: The lack of a committed timeline means Beyond Zero should be treated as a directional signal for the security market rather than a near-term product to underwrite investment decisions around.
insights.locator: Google presents Beyond Zero as an ongoing effort
